desc:
You are given an array nums of distinct positive integers. Two numbers are linked if they share a common divisor greater than 1 (their gcd is at least 2). Numbers are also in the same group when a chain of linked numbers connects them: if a is linked to b and b to c, then all three are in one group, even if a and c are coprime.

Return the size of the largest group. The number 1 shares no divisor above 1 with anything, so it is always alone.

nums = [4,6,15,35]               -> 4   (4-6 via 2, 6-15 via 3, 15-35 via 5)
nums = [20,50,9,63]              -> 2   ({20,50} via 10 and {9,63} via 9)
nums = [2,3,6,7,4,12,21,39]      -> 8
nums = [1,2,3]                   -> 1
hints: Checking gcd for every pair is O(n²) gcd calls. Is there a better way to know which numbers are linked?
Two numbers are linked exactly when they share a prime factor. So instead of linking numbers with numbers, link every number with its prime factors.

Factor each number by trial division with primes up to √100,000. Union-find over the number indices: remember for each prime the first index that had it, and union every later number with that index. Count the group sizes at the end.
editorial: If two numbers share a common divisor d > 1 they also share a prime factor of d, so linking is equivalent to sharing a prime. For every number, factorise it and, for each prime p, union the number's index with owner[p], the first number seen that contained p (or record the number as owner). Numbers that contain several primes thereby glue those primes' groups together.

Afterwards count the members of every root and take the maximum. Trial division by the 65 primes below 317 factorises any value up to 100,000. Total time is about O(n · π(√V)) for factoring plus nearly linear union-find work. The pairwise-gcd method is O(n² log V) and too slow for n = 5,000.
